intro:
This track spreads one store's data over many machines. Lessons start from scenes everyone knows, such as a café's card reader on the busiest shopping day of the year, six friends cutting a pizza, a cloakroom with three attendants or a box office with one long queue. Then they open up the machinery, on real clusters running on your laptop.

By the end, you can:

- say why copies stop helping once data outgrows one machine, and cut it into shards by key range, by hash or by customer;
- spot a key that will pile every new payment onto one machine, and split a key that's too busy for any machine;
- count what moves when a machine joins, and follow a request to a payment that moved a minute ago;
- say how many shards a question asks when it doesn't carry the key, and why asking more of them makes the slowest answers slower;
- explain how Cassandra, MongoDB, DynamoDB and OpenSearch each keep their map, place their copies and react when a machine stops.

The nine lessons:

1. Splitting data: key ranges, hashes and tenants
2. Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys
3. Rebalancing and request routing
4. Secondary indexes across shards: local and global
5. Inside a Cassandra cluster: the token ring, gossip and failure detection
6. Setting up and running a Cassandra cluster
7. Running MongoDB: replica sets, sharding and the balancer
8. DynamoDB under the hood: partitions, routers and capacity
9. Inside a search cluster: OpenSearch nodes, shards and replicas

The first four lessons build the ideas. The last five are case studies, and each one opens by naming the ideas it puts together.

You need to read a little code, in Kotlin or Java, and to have Docker on your laptop. Docker is a free program that runs small, separate Linux systems, called containers, on your own computer. Take the Replication track first: leaders and followers, quorums and copies that fall behind come back in every lesson. The Data models track's key designs for DynamoDB, Cassandra and MongoDB are the tables these lessons spread over machines. Every term is explained the first time a lesson uses it, and where a lesson leans on Raft, which the Consensus track builds later, it says what it needs on the spot.

Every lab is a package, `sfz.shard.l01` to `sfz.shard.l09`, and needs only the JDK. The case studies' labs (lessons 5 to 9) live in `labs/nosql`, and each lesson's lab names its module. You build a range router and a hash router with customers placed on cells, a hash ring with virtual nodes, gossip and a failure detector, placement of copies across racks, a model of Cassandra's data movement checked against a real join's log, a MongoDB shard-key simulator, a DynamoDB partition and capacity model, and a search cluster that routes, places copies and survives a failure. Run `./gradlew :nosql:test --tests 'sfz.shard.l05.*'` from `labs/` for one lesson; the finished answers live in `src/solution`. The Try-its run real clusters in Docker (`env/cassandra-cluster.yml`, `env/mongo-sharded.yml`, `env/dynamodb.yml`, `env/opensearch-cluster.yml`, 2 to 4 GB each). Start one at a time, and stop it with `down -v` when the lesson ends.
cheatsheet:
## Why shard, and how to split

Shard, that is, split the data so each row lives on one machine, when the data won't fit on one machine or the writes are more than one leader can take. For reads, add copies first: sharding is heavy and hard to undo.

| Scheme | A key goes to | Good at | Breaks on | Used by | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Key range | the shard whose range holds the key | ranges of keys, sorted order | keys that only grow (times, counters): every insert hits the last range | MongoDB ranged keys, HBase, CockroachDB, Vitess | 1, 7 |
| Hash, `hash mod N` | the remainder of `hash(key)` divided by N | an even spread | changing N moves about N/(N+1) of the keys (80% from 4 to 5 nodes) | OpenSearch, per index (N fixed at creation) | 1, 3, 9 |
| Fixed shard count | one of a fixed set of shards, then a map from shard to node | moving whole shards; machines of different sizes | needing more nodes than shards | Citus, Riak, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch | 3 |
| Hash range | a range of hash values that splits when it gets big or busy | an even spread, automatic splits | ranges over the partition key | DynamoDB, MongoDB hashed keys, YugabyteDB | 1, 8 |
| Ring with virtual nodes | the first token clockwise from the key's hash | few keys move on a join, taken from many nodes | load: a busy key stays busy | Cassandra (16 tokens per node), ScyllaDB before tablets | 2, 5 |
| Customer (tenant) or cell | the shard that holds the customer | walls between customers; moving or deleting one at a time | one customer too big for one shard | cell-based services, Citus schema sharding | 1 |

A good partition key has many values, no value that dominates, doesn't only grow, and appears in the busiest questions. Even keys don't mean even load: one busy key (a shop's running total) lives on one shard. Write sharding spreads it over `key#0` to `key#9`, and makes every read ask all ten.

## Who holds the map, and how a request finds its shard

| System | The map lives in | A request finds its shard by | Data moves |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cassandra 5.0 | every node's own copy, kept in step by gossip | any node coordinates; drivers route by token | only when a person adds or removes a node |
| Cassandra 6.0 (alpha) | a log ordered by the Cluster Metadata Service, one epoch per change | the same | in logged steps: PREPARE_JOIN, START_JOIN, MID_JOIN, FINISH_JOIN |
| MongoDB 9.0 | the config server replica set (`config.chunks`) | `mongos` routers with a cached map; `StaleConfig` refreshes it | the balancer, when shards differ by 3 chunk sizes; `moveCollection`, `reshardCollection` |
| DynamoDB | MemDS, cached on the request routers | any router | splits by size, capacity and traffic; never merges |
| OpenSearch | the cluster state, changed only by the elected cluster manager | any node coordinates | placed and moved by the manager |
| Kafka 4.x | the KRaft controller quorum | clients fetch the map | reassignment tools |
| Redis Cluster | each node's slot map | the client's slot map, fixed by `-MOVED` and `-ASK` | slot migration |

Moving data automatically is convenient and dangerous: a slow node judged dead moves its load onto the others, and the overload spreads. Dynamo and Cassandra leave membership changes to a person for that reason.

## Secondary indexes across shards

| | Local: each shard indexes its own rows | Global: the index is split by the indexed value |
|---|---|---|
| Each shard indexes | its own rows only | one slice of the indexed values, for all rows |
| A write touches | one shard | the row's shard plus index shards (later, or in a transaction across machines) |
| A lookup by the indexed value | asks every shard and waits for the slowest | asks one index shard, then fetches the rows |
| Examples | MongoDB, Cassandra SAI, OpenSearch | DynamoDB GSIs (they lag, and can slow the table's writes), CockroachDB, TiDB |

The slowest shard sets the pace. If each of 10 shards answers in time 99 times in 100, a question to all 10 does so only 0.99^10, about 90%, of the time. A value that must be unique but isn't the key needs a global index, or a collection of its own keyed by that value.

## Membership and failure detection

| | Cassandra 5.0 gossip | SWIM (memberlist: Consul, Nomad, Serf) |
|---|---|---|
| Each period | Syn, Ack, Ack2 with one random peer, every second | ping one random member; if no answer, ask k others to ping it |
| Spreads | versioned state for each node; the generation (start time) wins after a restart | changes carried on the pings and their answers |
| Decides "down" | each node alone, with its phi accrual detector: phi = 0.434 x silence / average gap, down past 8 (about 18.4 average gaps) | suspect first; the member can answer back with a higher incarnation number |
| Cost | 3 messages per exchange; news reaches N nodes in about log N rounds | about 2 messages per member per period at any size; first detection after about 1.6 periods |

Lifeguard adds local health: a slow checker stretches its own timeouts, and a suspicion timeout shrinks as others confirm it. False alarms fell more than 50 times. Seeds only introduce new nodes, and a seed never bootstraps (copies data in as it joins).

## Numbers worth remembering

| What | Value |
|---|---|
| Cassandra | 16 tokens per node with `allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor: 3`; gossip every 1 s; `phi_convict_threshold` 8; hints kept 3 h; `gc_grace_seconds` 10 days; a join sleeps `ring_delay`, 30 s in 5.0; streaming 24 MiB/s per source |
| MongoDB | chunk 128 MB; the balancer acts at 3 chunk sizes (384 MB); an election after 10 s of silence, heartbeats every 2 s; oplog 5% of the disk, 990 MB to 50 GB; whole-collection moves take at least 5 minutes by default |
| DynamoDB | per partition 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second, about 10 GB; burst of up to 300 s of unused share; a new on-demand table takes 4,000 writes and 12,000 reads a second, then double the previous peak; quota 40,000 units per table |
| OpenSearch | shards of 10 to 50 GB; 1,000 shard copies per node; refresh every 1 s; `max_result_window` 10,000; a lost replica rebuilt after 1 min, at 40 MB/s; heap at most about 31 GB; disk marks at 85, 90 and 95% |

## Commands you'll reach for

```bash
nodetool status | ring | getendpoints <ks> <table> <key> | gossipinfo | failuredetector
nodetool cleanup | decommission | removenode <host id> | repair -pr | drain | snapshot -t <tag>
nodetool cms describe                                   # Cassandra 6.0: the metadata service and its epoch
```

```javascript
sh.status(); db.payments.getShardDistribution()
db.payments.find({ accountId: "A-1001" }).explain().queryPlanner.winningPlan.stage   // SINGLE_SHARD or SHARD_MERGE
db.adminCommand({ moveCollection: "sfz.merchants", toShard: "shard2" })
```

```bash
curl -s 'localhost:9200/_cat/shards?v'; curl -s 'localhost:9200/_cluster/health'
aws dynamodb put-item ... --return-consumed-capacity TOTAL   # then read ThrottlingReasons on errors
```
recap: Copies multiply only the reads: every copy stores every row and applies every write. When the data or the writes outgrow one machine, split the rows into shards, each row on exactly one, and give each shard its own copies. Sharding is hard to undo, so choose the key from the app's questions before the first split.

Key ranges keep neighbours together, and pile every new row onto the last shard when the key only grows, like a time. Hashes spread keys evenly and scatter the ranges. `hash mod N` moves almost every key when N changes, so real stores fix the number of shards, split ranges of hash values, or use a ring with many tokens per node.

Even keys aren't even load. One busy key lives on one shard whatever the cluster's size (1,000 write units a second per DynamoDB partition). Write sharding spreads it over several keys, and every read then asks them all.

Someone always holds the map of shards to machines: every node through gossip (Cassandra 5.0), one ordered log (Cassandra 6.0, Kafka), config servers behind routers (MongoDB), a metadata service behind routers (DynamoDB), or an elected manager (OpenSearch). A router with an old map gets turned away and refreshes it.

A local index keeps each write on one shard, and turns every other lookup into a question to all the shards, as slow as the slowest. A global index answers from one shard, but it updates later, or needs a transaction across machines.

Cassandra: every node works out a key's copies from its own map, gossip spreads news in about log N rounds, phi accrual calls a silent node down after about 18 average gaps, and a join copies each range from the node it replaces. Cleanup and repair are jobs a person must schedule.
SWIM checks one random member per period, through k others when a direct ping fails, and suspicion plus Lifeguard's local health keep a bad link or a slow checker from killing a healthy member.

MongoDB: a shard key that only grows sends every insert to the chunk that ends at MaxKey, and the balancer evens out stored data, not new writes. Since 8.0, `moveCollection` and `unshardCollection` move whole collections.

DynamoDB splits partitions by size and traffic, but no split lifts a partition's ceiling. OpenSearch fixes the number of primaries per index, promotes replicas when a node fails (yellow), and goes red only when every copy of a shard is gone.

quiz.q: A payments app is slow because its one main database machine, a PostgreSQL primary, is busy answering reads. Writes are 300 a second and the data is 200 GB. A teammate proposes sharding. What do you suggest first?
options: Add read replicas, copies that answer reads, and send them the reads that can be a little out of date; sharding is for data that won't fit or writes one leader can't take
Shard by account id over four machines
Shard by payment date, so old data lives elsewhere
Use consistent hashing, so adding machines later is cheap
quiz.why: Sharding is for data volume and write throughput. Here both are small, and the load is reads, which copies handle without sharding's costs: questions that cross shards, transactions across machines, and a key that's expensive to change later. A date key would also put every new write on one shard. Consistent hashing only makes sense once you're sharding at all.

quiz.q: A ledger table is split by key range on `created_at`, the time each row was written, over 8 shards whose boundaries split automatically. What happens at the peak, 5,000 inserts a second?
options: About 625 inserts a second on each shard
All 5,000 land on the shard holding the newest range, because every new row is later than all the others
The router spreads them in turn, and the balancer sorts them later
Splitting cuts the busy range, so the load spreads within seconds
quiz.why: A key that only grows sends every insert to the end of the key range, which one shard owns. Splits and balancing move the old data away, but the newest range is always in one place, as MongoDB's MaxKey chunk showed. Splitting the busy range only moves the end along, which is why the last option fails. A hashed first part, such as the account id, spreads the inserts.

quiz.q: A cache cluster places keys with `hash(key) % N`, the remainder after dividing the key's hash by the number of nodes. It grows from 10 nodes to 11. About what share of the keys now map to a different node?
options: About 9%: one eleventh
About 50%
About 91%: a key stays only when hash mod 10 equals hash mod 11
None: the hash doesn't change
quiz.why: For a key to stay, `h % 10` must equal `h % 11`, which holds for about 1 key in 11, so about 91% move. One eleventh is what a good design moves: consistent hashing moves only the new node's fair share, which is why rings, fixed shard counts and hash ranges that split replaced the plain remainder.

quiz.q: A sharded app looks payments up by card fingerprint, which isn't the shard key, and every shard keeps a local index on the fingerprint. There are 20 shards, and each answers within 15 ms 99 times in 100. Why is the lookup itself slower than 15 ms far more often than 1 time in 100?
options: A local index is slower than a global one on each shard
The router sends the 20 requests one after another
Each shard rebuilds its local index on every query
The lookup must ask all 20 shards and wait for the slowest; all 20 answer within 15 ms only 0.99^20, about 82%, of the time
quiz.why: A local index says nothing about other shards, so a lookup by anything but the key asks every shard and inherits the worst one's delay. 18% of lookups are slow, though each shard is slow only 1% of the time. A global index on the fingerprint answers from one index shard, at the cost of index writes that happen later or in a transaction, as DynamoDB's GSIs show.

quiz.q: Which statement about who holds a cluster's map of shards is true?
options: In Cassandra 5.0 every node holds a copy kept in step by gossip; in 6.0 it moves to a log ordered by the Cluster Metadata Service
Cassandra 5.0 keeps it on its seed nodes
MongoDB's mongos routers store it on disk, and their copy is the truth
OpenSearch lets any node change the routing table
quiz.why: Cassandra 5.0 nodes each keep the whole map and gossip versioned changes, and 6.0's Transactional Cluster Metadata puts membership, tokens and schema in one log of epochs. Seeds only introduce new nodes, mongos only caches the config servers' map and stores nothing on disk, and only OpenSearch's elected cluster manager changes the cluster state.

quiz.q: A Cassandra node freezes for 40 seconds while Java cleans up its memory (a garbage-collection pause). Its peers' heartbeats normally arrive about once a second. What do the other nodes do?
options: Mark it down after one missed gossip round
Each node marks it down on its own after about 18 to 20 seconds, when phi passes 8, then keeps hints for its writes; nobody moves its data
The seeds decide it's down and tell everyone, and its ranges stream to other nodes
Nothing, until a person runs `nodetool removenode`
quiz.why: Phi accrual compares the silence with the average gap and calls the node down at phi 8, about 18.4 average gaps, and each node decides for itself. Down means no reads sent there and hints (writes kept for it) for later, never a move: only a person changes the ring, which rules out the third option. When the frozen node wakes, a guard against its own pause stops it from calling everyone else down.

quiz.q: In a cluster that uses SWIM, a way of checking members by pinging them, member A's pings to member B time out because a firewall rule drops packets between those two machines only. Why isn't B declared dead?
options: B's phi stays under 8
SWIM never declares members dead
A retries the direct ping until it gets through
A asks k other members to ping B; their answers come back through them, so the broken link is routed around
quiz.why: Indirect pings are SWIM's defence against a bad link between two members. Only if those fail too is B suspected, and B can still answer back with a higher incarnation number. Phi belongs to Cassandra's detector, not SWIM's. Lifeguard adds the other half: a slow or overloaded checker stretches its own timeouts.

quiz.q: A Cassandra cluster grows from 6 to 9 nodes, with 3 copies of every row. A week later, the six old nodes' disks are as full as before. Why, and what's the fix?
options: Old nodes keep the rows of the ranges they handed over until `nodetool cleanup` rewrites their files; run it on each old node, one at a time
Streaming failed; rebuild the new nodes
Compaction is behind; give it more speed
Hints for the new nodes are piling up
quiz.why: A join copies each range from the node it replaces and deletes nothing on the old owners. Cleanup is a special compaction that drops the ranges a node no longer holds copies of. Normal compaction keeps every row, so speeding it up changes nothing, and the new nodes showing UN (up and normal) means the streams worked.

quiz.q: A provisioned DynamoDB table may take 40,000 write units a second and uses 6,000, but writes to one running-total item, 1,500 a second, are throttled with `TableWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded`. What fixes it?
options: Raise the table to 80,000 write units
Switch the table to on-demand
Spread the item over several keys (write sharding) and add them up on read; one key lives in one partition, capped at 1,000 write units
Wait for adaptive capacity to split the item
quiz.why: The table's capacity is a sum of partition ceilings, and one item can't be split. Adaptive capacity can give the item a partition of its own, but that partition still tops out at 1,000 write units, in either capacity mode, so neither more units nor on-demand helps. A `KeyRange` reason means a problem with the key, not with a capacity setting.

quiz.q: An OpenSearch index has 3 primaries and 1 replica on 3 nodes. Two nodes fail together, before any copy is rebuilt. What is the most likely state?
options: Green: replicas are promoted
Yellow: every primary has a node and some replicas don't
Red: with two copies per shard on three nodes, some shard had both copies on the two failed nodes, so its documents can't be searched
Searches return everything, but writes fail
quiz.why: One node failing is yellow: the manager promotes replicas, and every document stays searchable. With one replica, each shard's two copies sit on two of the three nodes, so any pair of failed nodes holds both copies of some shard. That's red until a node with the data returns or a snapshot is restored. A second replica would survive two failures.
